Boundary of use: what follows shows the same submissions read with different emphasis by two people; it is not a division of work by type. The actual split follows the work, printing experience, the resources that season and the agreed responsibilities; who takes which segment has nothing to do with four letters.

On a merchandise project, decide who owns the theme, who signs off on the proof and who can pause spending. Either person can consider the theme and check the proof. Allocate responsibilities by experience, availability and authority.

### ENFP and ISFP: choosing the style of merchandise illustrations

(Fictional scene) A canvas tote and stickers, four illustrators submitting, the printer wanting files in ten days. One may treat the four as four world views, think about which could grow a second season and become a whole set, lean toward the incomplete one whose direction is right, and be willing to ask the illustrator for another round. The other may look at the line and the feel, at whether it is still recognisable shrunk to sticker size, at whether it will go grey on canvas, and lean toward the one that is right already, even if the series potential is weaker.

The cost runs both ways. Choosing the right direction may mean not finishing in ten days and delivering something half-made; choosing the one that is right now may mean a set with no next season and no repeat purchase. Both costs are real and unrelated to type; they relate to deadline, budget and what this season is for.

Print the illustrations at the intended size. For each recommended change, note what evidence supports it, what the trade-off is and what new information would change your mind. Either person can flag a theme or a specific shape. The exercise clarifies the design decision.

Check whether the illustrator understands the change and can test it in the next proof. Clear feedback is useful because it can be acted on, not because it reveals someone’s type.

### ENFP and ISFP: telling the illustrator to make it cuter

(Fictional scene) The same request can be phrased very differently. One may say they want it looser, more like something a child drew casually; the illustrator may be more lost in the moment, but the sentence can open an entirely new direction. The other may take a pen and circle on the printout — the corner radius two millimetres larger here, this eye moved down a little — or simply trace a version themselves to show.

Both carry risk. The first gives space, and may give an expectation that cannot be delivered; the second can be executed immediately, and may wipe out the illustrator's own handling. A workable approach says what to keep first, then what to change, breaking "cute" into two or three pointable parts — corner radius, eye position, line weight.

Either person can give broad or precise feedback. How specific the note is can reflect what the team already agreed, how much time is available and whether the writer has found the right words.

### ENFP and ISFP: going with a friend to look at tattoo designs

(Fictional scene) A friend wants a Latin phrase tattooed on the inner forearm and takes both along to the shop to look at designs. This is not a judgement about whether he should get it, and it does not give professional advice on the shop's behalf; what, how and aftercare are for him and the shop to decide according to professional guidance. What can be helped with is asking the questions fully.

In the fictional visit, either friend can ask what the phrase means, whether there are other ways to express it and what the artist’s portfolio shows. The person considering the tattoo can take questions about placement, care and removal to the relevant professionals.

The friends can discuss possible designs and the evidence in the portfolio without assigning either role by type. The order of their questions cannot distinguish ENFP from ISFP.

They can agree to use the visit to ask questions and leave the decision for later. The choice belongs to the person considering the tattoo.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
Message volume and time spent talking cannot establish E/I. Either type can be animated with people they know or quiet in an unfamiliar setting.

The second takes having firm views for T. Both lean F, and both may hold a position for a long time over a reason they cannot articulate; holding firm is not evidence of Thinking or Feeling. In the other direction, both can hold out when asked to accept a conclusion that does not make sense.

The third takes being good with your hands for S. An ISFP may never make anything and still be exacting about the finished product; an ENFP may sketch their own drafts. Whether someone can make things is the result of training and experience, with no correspondence to where material is gathered.

The fourth uses the abstraction of one piece of feedback to define a person. The same "make it cuter" may mean the words have not been found, or may be a professional shorthand; look at how they talk on other occasions, and whether they had the authority and the time to request changes then.

- [ENFP: base preferences led by extraverted Intuition](/en/personality/enfp)
- [ISFP: base preferences led by introverted Feeling](/en/personality/isfp)
- [Browse the 16 types: compare other base descriptions](/en/personality)

A/T further reading: 16Personalities' NERIS Identity, covering self-evaluation, self-assurance and response to pressure, not a fifth official MBTI dimension. A stands for Assertive, T for Turbulent; it is a different frame from the four letters above, so it is listed separately.

- [ENFP-A](/en/personality/enfp-a) · [ENFP-T](/en/personality/enfp-t) · [ISFP-A](/en/personality/isfp-a) · [ISFP-T](/en/personality/isfp-t)

FermatMind MBTI preference assessment (a separate item bank and scoring): [FermatMind MBTI preference assessment](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types)

If only one of the two differing axes stays unclear, the [INFP profile](/en/personality/infp) can be used to check the letters one by one and keep the two axes apart.
